extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of Renaissance intellectual history; scholars of Erasmus and early-modern political thought
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes Erasmus's practical and moral criteria for rulers and public policy (taxation, war, appointments, education) as presented in the Institutio Principis Christiani and the author's commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of office not for private gain
rubrics_metrics.description: "The office of the prince is too lofty to be used for money-making. The good prince has for his own whatever his loving subjects have."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prince should not treat the position as a source of private revenue; public office should be exercised for the people's good rather than the ruler's enrichment. Example contrast given with ancient examples like Fabius Maximus and Antoninus Pius who sought only glory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and cutting unnecessary expense
rubrics_metrics.description: "The very best way to increase the revenue is to cut off unnecessary expense, doing away with burdensome service, avoiding wars and journeys that are like wars, checking the greed of officials, and trying rather to govern well what the prince has, than to get more."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fiscal policy should prioritize thrift and efficient governance over raising taxes; reduce administrative and military waste; check corrupt officials. Summarized proverb: 'Thrift is a great revenue.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Progressive and fair taxation burdening the least
rubrics_metrics.description: If necessity demands taxation, "it is the part of a good prince to do it in such a way that the least burden may fall upon those who have least."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid regressive taxes that hit the poor hardest; when levying taxes, protect the needy and place burdens on those better able to bear them. Avoid measures that compel the poor to hunger or lead to rebellion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tax necessities lightly; tax luxuries and foreign goods
rubrics_metrics.description: "Whatever things are in common use by the mass of the people, these a good prince will tax as lightly as possible... But if some duties cannot be avoided... let the burden fall upon foreign and outlandish wares... used by the rich alone, as for example, fine linen, silks, purple, perfumes, unguents, gems..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer indirect taxation on luxury and imported goods rather than essentials (corn, bread, beer, wine, clothing). This reduces hardship and may encourage frugality among the wealthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid and remedy corrupt precedents from emergency exactions
rubrics_metrics.description: An expense once incurred in an emergency "can never be abolished" unless remedied; the prince should "beware of the corrupt precedent" and remove burdens after the emergency is past.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temporary emergency levies should be rescinded and costs remedied afterward; failure to remove such measures creates lasting unjust burdens and political danger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oppose monopolies and multiple layers of exaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Present heavy burdens arise from "the very heavy exactions of the contractors ... duties which have also their contractors, and finally by monopolies which bring little to the prince, but crush the poor by higher prices."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid outsourcing revenue collection to contractors who extract rents and foster monopolies that raise prices for essentials while delivering little to the public treasury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent excessive inequality of wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: "It ought to be provided for that there be not too great inequality of wealth; -- not that I would have anyone deprived of his goods by force, but that care should be taken lest the wealth of the whole community be limited to a certain few."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public policy should discourage extreme concentration of wealth (without forcible dispossession) because both very poor and very rich are less useful to the state; social and fiscal measures should promote a broadly-based prosperity.

rubrics_metrics.name: War only as last resort; prioritize people's advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: "War should not be undertaken until all other methods of composing differences shall have failed... The good prince measures all things by the advantage of the people... Why not rather resort to arbiters?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage in military action only after exhausting diplomacy and arbitration; weigh the costs to the populace and avoid wars arising from private disputes of princes. Promote arbitration by bishops, abbots, scholars, and magistrates as alternatives to war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatic pursuit of 'right' measured against public cost
rubrics_metrics.description: "By all means let right be pursued, if this be of advantage to the state, but let not the right of the prince be too costly to the people."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal or honor-based claims should be pursued only when their pursuit serves the common good and does not impose intolerable costs on the people; concessions and compromise can be virtues to preserve public welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral primacy of the prince as servant of the people
rubrics_metrics.description: Erasmus's central view: the prince is "only as the servant of his people" and "the higher moral function of the ruler" matters more than mere expediency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruler's legitimacy and long-term success rest on moral conduct: governing for the people's benefit, seeking enduring rather than momentary advantage, and grounding policy in moral obligation rather than pure expediency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid advisors who propose cheating the people
rubrics_metrics.description: "There are men who busy themselves with nothing but finding out new devices for cheating the people... Let him who listens to them know that he is far from the true ideal of a prince."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware counselors who recommend exploitative schemes; a good ruler should distrust proposals that enrich the crown at the people's expense and cultivate honest, public-minded advisors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer native-language teachers for correct pronunciation
rubrics_metrics.description: In appointing the Greek professorship: "it has always been my opinion that a native Greek should be procured, so that the hearers may get the correct pronunciation at once."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When founding language chairs, prioritize native speakers for teaching pronunciation and authenticity. Offer fair salary, travel costs, and lodgings; rely on personal recommendation and trustees' judgment to secure suitable scholars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications for a Hebrew teacher (scholarly excellence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendation of Adrian: "he is a Hebrew by birth... so skilled in the whole Hebrew literature that in my judgment there is no one at this day to be compared with him... not only knows the language perfectly, but is thoroughly acquainted with the mysteries of the authors and has them all at his fingers' ends."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select teachers with deep textual mastery and broad acquaintance with scholarly traditions; reputation among peers can corroborate suitability. Practical considerations (salary, lodging, travel) should be provided to secure top candidates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly freedom bounded by doctrinal orthodoxy and common sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Erasmus's principle: freedom of speech kept "carefully within the bounds of doctrinal orthodoxy" and guided by "the principle of common sense working upon the accepted dogmatic bases of the existing church system."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intellectual critique and scholarship should operate with prudence: seek reform and critical inquiry while avoiding overt heresy; rely on sound judgment and the prevailing doctrinal framework to maintain influence and protection.
